findings.text: §1 caches a resolved short citation "under its tree and the candidate as written, whatever its length" in `_RESOLVE_COMMIT_CACHE` and the persistent `recovery_watch` store, but the guard it removes is documented at recovery_review_subject.py:205-209 as existing precisely because "a ref name or an abbreviation can move, so neither is ever kept"; the replacement key carries only tree and candidate, with no head or object-store identity, so an abbreviation whose referent changes (a fetched object making the prefix ambiguous, or a worktree path reused at a different revision) returns the stale commit forever — and the persistent store survives process exit, so nothing re-asks.

findings.text: the §1 followup body says "§1 stops each follower starting git every second: it re-derives its code identity only when HEAD moves", which describes behaviour the plan's own intro (line 40) says already exists in `checkout_trust._identity_hold` and is "not a cost here", while §1 actually memoises short-sha resolutions in `_resolve_commit`; the followup is the text a coordinator reads to decide what the dispatch delivers.

findings.text: §1 states an unresolved citation "is remembered only against the reading of `git_head._head_identity` for that tree, so a commit that arrives later is asked about again once HEAD or its ref moves", but `_head_identity` (reckon/git_head.py:82-107) reads only `HEAD` and the ref it names, so an object fetched into the repository without advancing that ref leaves the negative answer cached.

findings.reason: the two files are tiny and the choice is a one-token edit, but a worker following the text as written exceeds a binding host limit, so it is worth correcting in passing.
